faqs.question: What are the main types of Diwali card?
faqs.answer: Five: a shop-bought printed card, a handmade card, a digital image card sent on WhatsApp or Instagram, an interactive card page sent as a link, and a printed card with a link or QR code inside. They differ most on lead time and on how the card is kept, not on the wish.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a digital Diwali card and an interactive one?
faqs.answer: A digital card is a single image the recipient looks at once. An interactive card is a web page they do something in, such as lighting diyas or opening a letter, and SubhSandesh pages average 11.1 views each (measured 24 September 2026), so people go back to them.

faqs.question: Did India Post ever sell its own Diwali greeting cards?
faqs.answer: Yes. In September 2000 the Department of Posts launched "Greeting Post", cards sold in envelopes with an embossed prepaid stamp at ₹12 or ₹15 including postage, with 32 designs developed for Diwali, so the buyer did not need a separate envelope and stamp.

faqs.question: When should I post a Diwali card for Diwali 2027?
faqs.answer: Lakshmi Puja falls on Friday 29 October 2027, so post by about Wednesday 20 October. India Post publishes no festival-week delivery time, so a week of margin is the safe assumption.

faqs.question: Is a handmade Diwali card worth the effort?
faqs.answer: For parents and grandparents receiving one from a grandchild, yes: it costs about ₹100–400 in materials for a batch (EST, October 2026) and one to three hours a card. For a long list of colleagues it is the wrong tool, and an image card does the job.

faqs.question: How does a paper Diwali card with a link inside work?
faqs.answer: A printed card with a short link or QR code written inside, pointing to a digital card. You post the paper about a week early and finish the page on Diwali itself, because a SubhSandesh page can be edited and republished at the same link.

faqs.question: What should I send a grandparent who does not use a smartphone?
faqs.answer: A printed or handmade card posted by about 20 October 2027, followed by a phone call on the evening of Friday 29 October. Any link-based card assumes a screen they do not have.

faqs.question: Which type of Diwali card is most likely to be kept?
faqs.answer: Paper. Printed Diwali cards last long enough for the Victoria and Albert Museum to hold examples from 1998 and 2000, while an image card usually sinks in a chat within the day.

faqs.question: What size should a printed Diwali card be?
faqs.answer: Around 16 × 11 cm is a common greeting-card size: the V&A's 1998 Diwali card measures 16.3 × 11.7 cm. Weigh anything carrying pearls or glitter at the post office counter before posting it, since heavier cards cost more to send.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Which Diwali Card to Send: Paper, Handmade, Digital, Interactive

A Diwali card now comes in five forms: a shop-bought printed card, a handmade card, a digital image card, an interactive card page, and a printed card with a link inside. Pick by three things, not by design: how far away the person is, what screen they use, and whether they keep cards. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone (27,725 of 57,456 views, measured 24 September 2026), and the average page is viewed 11.1 times, counting repeat views rather than unique visitors.

Those two numbers are the case for a card that lives on a phone and gets reopened, while paper still wins on the mantelpiece. Below are the five types with cost, start date for Diwali on Friday 29 October 2027, and the right recipient for each.

## What is a Diwali card today?

A Diwali card is a greeting sent for the festival of lights, carrying a wish and usually a festival symbol such as a diya, Lakshmi, a rangoli or fireworks. For most of its history that meant printed paper; today the same greeting can travel as paper, as an image file, or as a web page that opens on the recipient's phone.

The printed card has enough history to sit in a museum. The Victoria and Albert Museum holds a [1998 Diwali card by Kiran Ahmad, printed by Setu Ltd in England](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O85161/), gold embossing on white card measuring 16.3 × 11.7 cm, with a four-armed goddess releasing gold coins that the museum links to Gujarati Lakshmi worship. A [second V&A card, published in 2000 by The Publishing House](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1172046/), is catalogued as evidence that Britain's mainstream card industry had added Diwali to its festival range.

## Five types of Diwali card, and who each one suits

Each type gets the same four fields in the same order: what it is, who it suits, cost and time. Prices are rough Indian estimates for October 2026, marked EST.

### 1. Shop-bought printed card

A folded, printed card with an envelope from a stationer or online shop, usually near the V&A card's 16 × 11 cm. It suits grandparents and elders who stand cards on a shelf, and anyone you will meet in person during the five days.

Expect roughly ₹50–300 per card (EST), plus postage if it travels. India Post once sold the whole package: its "Greeting Post" range, launched in September 2000, put each card in an envelope with an embossed prepaid stamp at ₹12 or ₹15 including postage, with 32 designs drawn for Diwali, according to the [Press Information Bureau release](https://archive.pib.gov.in/archive/releases98/lyr2000/rsep2000/r06092000.html). Writing takes ten minutes; delivery takes days you do not control.

### 2. Handmade card

Paper, colour pens, sometimes pearls or glitter, made by you or a child. On 22 October 2026 the top two India results for "diwali card" were a craft tutorial video and a craft pin. It suits parents and grandparents receiving a card from a grandchild, and a partner who saves things.

Materials for a batch of five or six run about ₹100–400 (EST), and each card takes one to three hours. It still has to be posted or handed over, so paper's delivery problem applies.

### 3. Digital image card

A single designed picture, a JPG or PNG, sent on WhatsApp, Instagram or email, often with the recipient's name set into it. It suits the long list: colleagues, old school friends, the extended family group.

There is no printing or postage, and a ready design takes two to five minutes to personalise. The weakness is shelf life: an image lands in a chat between dozens of other festival forwards, and nobody goes back to it on 30 October.

### 4. Interactive card page

A private web link that opens into something the recipient does, lighting, tapping and opening things, rather than a picture they look at once. It suits one person or a small household: a partner, parents in another city, a sibling abroad.

There is no printing or postage, and SubhSandesh's Diwali template takes about five minutes by its own how-to. It arrives instantly, and pages on the platform average 11.1 views each, a reopening that an image in a chat rarely gets.

### 5. Printed card with a link inside

A paper card with a short link or QR code written or stuck inside, pointing to a digital card. It suits elders who love a physical card but own a smartphone, and family abroad who will receive the paper late anyway.

The cost is the printed card plus postage. Post the paper a week early and finish the page on the day: a SubhSandesh page can be edited and republished, and the same link always shows the latest version.

## Diwali card types compared: cost, lead time and keeping

This compares the five types on money, start date for 29 October 2027, keeping, and what SubhSandesh has measured.

| Card type | Cost per card (EST, Oct 2026) | Start by, for 29 Oct 2027 | How it is kept | SubhSandesh measurement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shop-bought printed | ₹50–300 + postage | Post by about 20 Oct | Shelf, then a drawer | None; 49.4% of Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages were built on the day, too late for post |
| Handmade | ₹100–400 materials per batch | Start about 15 Oct | Shelf or a keepsake box | None measured |
| Digital image | No print or post | Same day | Buried in a chat | None; sent outside the platform |
| Interactive page | No print or post | Same day, about 5 minutes | A link that keeps working | 11.1 views per page, repeat views included |
| Printed card + link | Printed card + postage | Post about 20 Oct, finish page any time | Both | 38.5% of creators password-protect, so the paper can carry the password |

The takeaway: paper wins on keeping and loses on lead time, while the two digital types are the only ones that still work if you decide on the day.

## How to choose a Diwali card for family

Three questions settle it for almost every relative. Do they live nearby, use a smartphone daily, and keep their cards?

- **Nearby, any device:** a printed or handmade card handed over during the five days.
- **Far away, smartphone user:** an interactive page for parents and siblings, an image card for the extended group.
- **Far away, no smartphone:** a printed card posted by about 20 October, with a phone call on the evening of 29 October.
- **Far away, smartphone, keeps every card:** the hybrid, a posted card with a link and the password written inside.

## Timing each Diwali card type for 29 October 2027

Diwali 2027 runs from Dhanteras on Wednesday 27 October to Bhai Dooj on Sunday 31 October, with Lakshmi Puja on Friday 29 October. A paper card meant for Lakshmi Puja should leave by about Wednesday 20 October; that week of margin is a working assumption for festival-week post, not a published delivery time.

Most people decide much later than that. SubhSandesh's nearest festival data is Raksha Bandhan 2026, used here as an analogue with only 89 pages: 49.4% were built on the festival day itself, 27.0% the day before, and none more than 7 days ahead.

If you are in that 49.4%, paper is off the table by the time you decide. The fallback is a digital card that evening, or the hybrid with paper posted early and the page finished late.

## Where SubhSandesh's interactive Diwali card fits

SubhSandesh's Diwali template is type 4 from the list above. The recipient finds a diya at their door with a tag from you, lights a row of wish diyas, colours a rangoli until your initials glow, writes with a sparkler, lights sky lanterns holding up to six of your photos, plays with drawn crackers that make no noise or smoke, opens a letter from a red-and-gold shagun liffafa, and ends at a box of mithai and a Shubh Deepavali card.

You choose love, family or friend mode, add a YouTube song or a Diwali favourite, and can let the AI write from a short story about the two of you. If that is the card you want, start with [SubhSandesh's interactive Diwali card with photos and music](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali); it opens in any browser with no app or account, and the closing card saves as a 1080×1920 image.

For parents far away who would rather hear you than tap through scenes, try the [Dedication page, a radio show that plays your real voice introducing a song](https://subhsandesh.in/dedication). It is not a Diwali design, so the festival has to come from what you say.

## When a paper card, or no card, beats a link

Volume is the first case. A randomised study in the BMJ sent [Christmas cards to clinical trial participants](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8669570) and, across 1,469 people analysed, found no difference in follow-up: 85.3% with a card against 85.4% without, at £0.76 and about 140 g of CO2 per card.

A card sent as routine to a long list changes little, whatever the medium. For 200 contacts an image card is enough.

The second case is a recipient with no smartphone or no habit of opening links, since a page that 48.3% of recipients open on a phone is built for a screen they may not own. The third is sharing a house on 29 October, where a handed-over card beats any link; and anyone who keeps a box of old Diwali cards should get paper for the box.

structuralLimitations: No Diwali usage data exists; the post uses platform-wide lines (48.3% phone opens, 11.1 views per page, 38.5% passwords) and the Raksha Bandhan 2026 lead-time analogue (n = 89), labelled as such in the body.

No peer-reviewed study of Diwali cards or of printed vs digital festival greetings in India was found (findpapers: 'electronic greeting cards versus paper greeting cards', 'greeting cards history India Diwali', 'handwritten note recipient perception warmth', 'physical versus digital gift preference'; Europe PMC 'Christmas cards', 'festival greetings'). The BMJ Christmas-card RCT is the closest open-access greeting-card trial. Reshadi, Givi & Das (2023, Psychology & Marketing) on digital vs physical gift cards was dropped in the Phase 8 fix pass: Wiley (abs and pdfdirect), the IIM Bangalore repository (Sucuri JS challenge) and the Semantic Scholar page all refused automated fetches, and the abstract existed only in Crossref/OpenAlex API records, which are not reader-facing pages.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The India top 10 for 'diwali card' holds no editorial page at all, so this is the only result that answers which type of card to send, with a 2027 posting deadline, a dated piece of India Post history (the 2000 'Greeting Post' range with 32 Diwali designs) and SubhSandesh's own reopen and lead-time numbers. The fix pass made every source keyword-specific but cost the post two things: it no longer quotes current postage rates, and it lost the only study on whether recipients mind digital cards, so the case for digital to family now rests on platform-wide behaviour and a Raksha Bandhan analogue (n = 89), not Diwali data. It cannot overcome the commercial intent of the head term: shops, Canva and stock libraries own the clicks for people who want to buy or design a card, and the domain has far less authority, so any visibility is likely to come from answer engines and the long-tail secondaries rather than position one.
